items.title: William Russell Interview, 1976-02-16
items.q: I think Lee Collins would say that was Buddy Petit used to play that almost note for note, like Cornet Chop Suey.

ctx.x: Yeah, he called it, said that's novelty style. It wasn't, and yet they probably played at times that way here too. I imagine Louie probably, because people talk about, when they talk about like Cornet Chop Suey, they'll say, well, the first people, first person they ever heard play that. I think Lee Collins would say that was Buddy Petit used to play that almost note for note, like Cornet Chop Suey. Which is, largely features the trumpet, you know, not all the way through. But of course, even there they have a…

Well, maybe the strict ensemble style, in a sense, or I don't know how you feel about this, kind of sold the seeds of its own destruction, like many styles do that have a, that are quite, they have a pretty formal pattern to them. And they're, they're quite strict in that, that they just don't last forever because of the, I mean, you know, I don't know.

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1975-02-02
items.q: He modeled his tone after Bunk and after Buddy Petit.

ctx.x: What about— Well, anyway, I guess if there's anything else to talk about.

So again, as I say, Lee did have a more beautiful open tone. He modeled his tone after Bunk and after Buddy Petit. Some people think that Lee Collins was a Louie imitator, which he always denied. He knew people said that about him. And he didn't resent it because he liked Louie and was a Louie fan and went to see Louie, I know, once when I was there with him at the Blue Note. So he was an idol of his, too, and took pride that he knew him and had played with him and all. But Lee always did deny that he was really…
Well, I could ask you something, uh, if you can talk about the— Chalks of musicians, who got the band together in 1944?
